From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
Countries with World Heritage Sites in danger. Number of sites indicated by colour:
*   Six or more sites

*   Five sites

*   Four sites

*   Three sites

*   Two sites

*   One site
The Church of the Nativity, traditionally thought to be the birthplace of Jesus, is one of several sites to have been designated as a World Heritage Site and World Heritage in Danger in the same year. In 2019 it was removed from the danger list.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-1)
The **List of World Heritage in Danger** is compiled by the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) through the World Heritage Committee, in accordance with Article 11.4 of the World Heritage Convention,[[nb 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-2) and was established in 1972 to designate and manage World Heritage Sites.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) The list includes sites that are under threat and whose conservation requires major interventions and for which "assistance has been requested".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-convention-3) It is intended to raise international awareness of these threats and to encourage counteractive measures against them.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-WHinDanger-4) Threats to a site can be either proven imminent threats or potential dangers to a site.

For natural sites, ascertained dangers include the serious decline in the population of an endangered or other valuable species, as well as the deterioration of a property's natural beauty or scientific value caused by human activities. These activities may include logging, pollution, settlement, mining, agriculture or major public works. For cultural properties, ascertained dangers include the serious deterioration of materials, structure, ornamentation, or architectural coherence, as well as the loss of historical authenticity or cultural significance. Potential dangers for both cultural and natural sites include development projects, armed conflicts, inadequate management systems or changes in the legal protective status of the properties. For cultural sites, gradual changes resulting from geological, climatic, or environmental factors may also be potential dangers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5)
Before a property is inscribed on the List of World Heritage in Danger, its condition is assessed and a potential programme for corrective measures is developed in cooperation with the State Party involved. The final decision about inscription is made by the committee. Financial support from the World Heritage Fund may be allocated by the committee for listed properties. The state of conservation is reviewed yearly, after which the committee may request additional measures, delete the property from the list if the threats have ceased or consider deletion from both the List of World Heritage in Danger and the World Heritage List.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-UNESCO-opguidelines-5) Of the three former UNESCO World Heritage Sites, the Dresden Elbe Valley and the Liverpool Maritime Mercantile City were delisted after placement on the List of World Heritage in Danger while the Arabian Oryx Sanctuary was directly delisted.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-7) Some sites have been designated as World Heritage Sites and World Heritage in Danger in the same year, such as the Church of the Nativity, traditionally considered to be the birthplace of Jesus.

As of May 2026, there are 53 sites (14 natural and 39 cultural) on the List of World Heritage in Danger. Arranged by UNESCO regions, 22 of the listed sites are in the Arab States, 12 in Africa, six in Latin America and the Caribbean, six in Asia and the Pacific, and seven in Europe and North America. The majority of the endangered natural sites (nine) are in Africa.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-9) The list encompasses sites identified as facing threats to their integrity, which may arise from natural disasters, armed conflict, neglect, pollution, unsustainable tourism, or other hazards. Among these sites, the impacts of armed conflict are evident in countries such as Syria, where several sites, including the Ancient City of Aleppo and the Ancient Villages of Northern Syria, endangered as a result of the Syrian civil war. In Africa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo has multiple listings due to threats such as military conflict and environmental degradation affecting its national parks.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-10)
In some cases, inclusion on the danger list has sparked conservation efforts and prompted the release of funds, benefitting sites such as the Galápagos Islands and Yellowstone National Park, both later removed from the List of World Heritage in Danger. Despite this, the list itself and UNESCO's implementation of it have been subject to criticism.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p87-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-timothy-p83-12) In particular, States Parties and other stakeholders have questioned the authority of the World Heritage Committee to designate a site as in danger without their consent.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p2-3-13)

Until 1992, when UNESCO set a precedent by placing several sites on the danger list against the wishes of the respective States Parties, such parties would typically submit a programme of corrective measures before a site was listed.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-chape-p86-14) Rather than being used solely for its intended purpose, the List of World Heritage in Danger is perceived by some states as a "blacklist" and, according to Christina Cameron, Professor at the School of Architecture and Canada Research Chair on Built Heritage at the University of Montreal, has been used as a political tool to get the attention of States Parties.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-thorsell-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p0-16)
The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has noted that UNESCO has, in a number of cases, referenced the List of World Heritage in Danger without formally inscribing a site, particularly where threats could be easily addressed by the State Party.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p18-19-17) The Union has also argued that the prolonged retention of sites on the danger list is questionable and that other mechanisms for conservation should be sought in such cases.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_World_Heritage_in_Danger#cite_note-iucn-p19-20-18)

## Cape York Peninsula, Australia
A rock art gallery in Quinkan Country in Australia's Cape York Peninsula depicts ancestor kangaroos and dingos. Suzanne Long/Alamy
Australia’s northernmost region is decorated by 20,000-year-old rock art depicting the mythology of Indigenous Australians, one of the world’s oldest continuous civilizations. A wild expanse of rainforest, wetlands and savanna in the state of Queensland, Cape York Peninsula covers more than 45,000 square miles, the same size as Pennsylvania.
Despite its vastness, the peninsula is home to only 17,000 people—more than half of whom are Indigenous Australians. Humans have inhabited Cape York for up to 37,000 years, and their deep history and lore is etched into this landscape. Rock art galleries across the peninsula, especially in Quinkan Country, depict humans, birds, fish, reptiles, dingoes, echidnas, Indigenous rituals and ancestral beings.
According to Indigenous lore, those latter, supernatural entities created our planet and gave Australia’s Indigenous people the customs, codes of conduct and mythology that still prevail. They also spawned Cape York’s sublime geographic features—boulder fields, dune systems, coastal salt flats, mangrove forests—all of which are key elements of the site, which has been on the UNESCO tentative list since 2024.
Last year, Australia’s biggest rock art site, Murujuga, a group of more than one million petroglyphs by Indigenous communities in remote Western Australia, earned World Heritage status. Soon, Cape York Peninsula could join it.
An official designation may convince more tourists to seek out this remote wonder. Cape York Peninsula begins about 100 miles north of the nearest city, Cairns, where travelers can rent a car to drive into the wilderness or fly to one of several small Cape York communities, including Bamaga, at its very tip.

## The Ringed Seal Archipelagos of Lake Saimaa, Finland
Saimaa ringed seals are a rare subspecies of seals that are landlocked. Siepmann/imageBROKER.com/Alamy
Fewer than 550 Saimaa ringed seals remain on Earth, with all of these endangered animals residing in Lake Saimaa, Finland’s largest lake. The population plummeted in the 1900s. But, thanks to conservation efforts, the species has now recovered so well that tourists can join boat tours to see these seals basking by the lake’s edge—an especially common sight during the warmer months of May and June.
Saimaa ringed seals are a rare subspecies of seals that are landlocked, due to their unique history. Some 9,500 years ago, after geological forces gradually disconnected Lake Saimaa from the Baltic Sea, these seals were left isolated in this body of freshwater. Since then, they’ve evolved to behave in ways that differ from most other seals. They are far more solitary, and yet they are the only type of seal that breeds and lives near human communities. Lake Saimaa is fringed by five small cities, including its main tourist hub, Savonlinna, which boasts a 15th-century castle and an array of hotels, bars and restaurants.
Lake Saimaa itself is extraordinary. Located in southeastern Finland, it is 112 miles long, 87 miles wide, dotted by about 14,000 islands, pierced by dozens of narrow straits and surrounded by sheltered bays perfect for ringed seal breeding.
While Lake Saimaa is sheeted by ice from December to April, tourists can kayak, fish, hike, swim and cycle its leafy fringes the rest of the year. Most tourists reach Savonlinna from the Finnish capital, Helsinki, which is about 155 miles to the southwest. They either fly, catch a train or bus, or rent a car to complete the four-hour drive.

## Real Felipe Fortress of Callao, Peru
Tourists can wander many parts of the 24-acre grounds of the Real Felipe Fortress of Callao. Leonid Andronov/Alamy
Peru’s magnificent Real Felipe Fortress of Callao was originally erected in 1542 as the regional headquarters of the occupying Spanish, who controlled swaths of Central and South America until the 1820s. Peru was Spain’s most valuable territory, so the Spanish built a commanding seaside fortification at the port of Callao, ten miles west of Lima, the capital.
That initial structure was one of thousands of buildings demolished in 1746 by an earthquake and subsequent tsunami, which also claimed more than 1,000 lives. It was rebuilt in the 1770s as a huge, pentagonal fort ringed by a moat, guarded by five bastions and surrounded by an outer stone wall measuring almost a mile long.
While the fort still holds functioning military structures, tourists can wander many parts of its 24-acre grounds. Two on-site museums exhibit military artifacts and explain the fort’s history. The complex was embroiled in Peru’s long fight for freedom from Spain, whose control of Peru, and the region more widely, effectively ended in 1826, when the Spanish surrendered this fortress. Nowadays, visitors to Callao can use its elevated perch to peer out at the same seas where Spanish ships once retreated over the horizon, leaving Peru independent once more.

## Gcwihaba Caves, Botswana
The Gcwihaba Caves have an impressive array of stalagmites, stalactites, helictites, flowstones and cave pearls. Horst Klemm/Greatstock/Alamy
The flat expanse of the Kalahari Desert stretches on and on across Botswana, until broken by dolomite hills along the Namibian border, in a remote, sparsely inhabited part of southern Africa. Burrowed into these peaks, known as the Aha Hills, are six unusual cave systems with memorable fossils and rock formations.
The Gcwihaba Caves are more than two million years old. They were little known until 1992, when researchers entered the caves and found fossilized bones as well as an impressive array of stalagmites, stalactites, helictites, flowstones and cave pearls. UNESCO describes its cave fossil deposits as “possibly the richest in southern Africa.”
Tourists can now cautiously explore Gcwihaba Caves, too. From Botswana’s capital, Gaborone, it is a slow, 630-mile journey, which requires a four-wheel-drive vehicle due to rough roads. Visitors can then stay at campsites near the caves.
Upon entering the caves, visitors must remain calm in a dark, eerie environment teeming with thousands of bats. Parts of this sprawling subterranean system are too cramped for humans, while other caverns soar up to 33 feet high.
Visitors can also hike through the surrounding hilly environment. Keen-eyed tourists may spot the rare Namaqua fig trees, which are special to this area, as well as barking geckos, tent tortoises and Rüppell’s parrots, though their vision can never match that of the barn owls inhabiting these remarkable caves.

Item updated: Oct 9, 2026 Item created October 1, 2026 at 9:52 PM Item updated October 9, 2026 at 1:24 PM

This layer shows the official boundary of Virunga National Park, downloaded from Protected Planet (WDPA site ID 478291), covering approximately 780,000 hectares. It stretches from north of Butembo down to Goma at its southern tip, where the park narrows closest to the city.

One detail worth noting, this specific WDPA record is formally registered under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance, rather than listed separately under a national park designation, even though it is commonly known and referred to as Virunga National Park. The boundary and area match the widely reported figures for the park, so it is used here as the standard reference shape for the park's extent.

In this project, the boundary is used purely as spatial context, to show that the charcoal production zone and nearby displacement sites sit inside, or just outside, the park's southern edge, close to Goma.

# Virunga National Park boundary Open in Map Viewer Official boundary of Virunga National Park in the Democratic Republic of Congo, used as the reference layer showing where the charcoal production zone and displacement sites sit relative to the park. Item updated: Oct 9, 2026 Item created October 1, 2026 at 9:52 PM Item updated October 9, 2026 at 1:24 PM

This layer shows the official boundary of Virunga National Park, downloaded from Protected Planet (WDPA site ID 478291), covering approximately 780,000 hectares. It stretches from north of Butembo down to Goma at its southern tip, where the park narrows closest to the city.

One detail worth noting, this specific WDPA record is formally registered under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance, rather than listed separately under a national park designation, even though it is commonly known and referred to as Virunga National Park. The boundary and area match the widely reported figures for the park, so it is used here as the standard reference shape for the park's extent.

In this project, the boundary is used purely as spatial context, to show that the charcoal production zone and nearby displacement sites sit inside, or just outside, the park's southern edge, close to Goma.

We need to answer: "Of the natural sites on the UNESCO list of World Heritage in Danger, only a few sites are located in one of the original members of the United Nations. In which country is the site with the largest reported area according to Protected Planet?"

So we need to find natural sites on the UNESCO list of world heritage in danger (i.e., natural sites on the danger list), check which of them are located in a country that is an original member of the United Nations (1945 founding members). Among those, determine which has the largest area reported by Protected Planet, and answer the country.

Thus steps:

1. Identify natural sites on the UNESCO world heritage list of danger (damaging). We saw list. Natural sites: what categories? In the list, natural sites are marked. Earlier text: natural sites with shades: e.g., Everglades National Park (USA) is a natural site; Virunga, Garamba, etc. The list shows natural sites in Danger list include: Everglades National Park (USA), Virunga National Park (DRC), Garamba National Park (DRC), Kahuzi-Biega National Park (DRC), Okapi Wildlife Reserve (DRC). Also other natural: The text earlier may include many. Let's analyze the list from source. In the list displayed, there are lines with "Natural site" presumably. In the web capture, the list shows entries but no color tag. But maybe we can identify by reading National/State: some entries like "Everglades National Park" is natural. "Virunga National Park" is natural, "Garamba" natural, "Kahuzi-Biega", "Okapi Wildlife Reserve", "Selous Game Reserve" maybe natural. Also maybe "Tropical Rainforest" (Indonesia) is natural. "Manovo-Gounda" (Central African Republic) is natural. "Mount Nimba Strict Nature Reserve" (Côte d'Ivoire, Guinea) is natural. "Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve" (Honduras) is natural? That is biosphere reserve, but maybe natural. "Air and Ténéré Natural Reserves" (Niger) is natural. "East Rennell" (Solomon Islands) is natural. "Boma-Badingilo Migratory Landscape" (South Sudan) may be natural? Actually Boma is migratory, could be natural. "Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge" (USA) is natural. "Aqaba Marine Reserve" (Jordan) natural. etc.

But the question narrows: only a few sites are located in one of the original members of the UN. So which national parks in danger list are in founding members. Founding members include many countries: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Belarus (now Russia?), Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Czechoslovakia (now Czech, Slovakia), Denmark, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, Ethiopia, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Liberia, Luxembourg, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Philippines, Poland, Portugal? No, Portugal was not a founding member; but as a US franchise. The list of original members includes Portugal? Actually Portugal joined later. There's a list of 51 original members. The list: Argentina, Australia, Belgium, Bolivia, Brazil, Byelorussian SSR, Canada, Chile, China, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, Egypt, El Salvador, Ethiopia, France, Greece, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Liberia, Luxembourg, Mexico, Netherlands, New Zealand, Nicaragua, Norway, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Philippines, Poland, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey, Ukraine, Union of South Africa, USSR, United Kingdom, United States, Uruguay, Venezuela, Yugoslavia. Note: Scotland? Actually UK.

Thus, among danger natural sites, those located in these founding members would include: USA (Everglades, Okefenokee). Canada? Not included in list. Australia? Monte. DRC? not founding. Indonesia? founding? no. Belgium? not in area list. etc. Also there are natural natural sites in existing danger list for countries that are founding members: USA, maybe Brazil? There is no natural site in danger list in Brazil. There is "Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge" (USA). "Everglades National Park" (USA). "Aqaba Marine Reserve" (Jordan) - not founding. "Selous Game Reserve" (Tanzania) - not founding. "An ancient" etc. So likely the only natural sites in danger list that are in founding members are the USA. So the site with largest area would be Everglades or Okefenokee. Which area is larger? We need to find Protected Planet reported area for each. Everglades: 6226.72 km2 (in 2026). Okefenokee: need Protected Planet data. Let's search Okefenokee.

# Okefenokee
## Plan Your Visit
*   March to October: Open daily 30 minutes before sunrise to 7:30 p.m.  
*   November to February: Open daily 30 minutes before sunrise to 5:30 p.m.
**Suwannee River Sill, The Pocket, and Kingfisher Landing**
Open daily from sunrise to sunset.
**All boats must be off the water no later than**:
*   March to October: 6:00 pm  
*   November to February: 4:00 pm
Visit Okefenokee State Park for state park specific hours.
Pass Details
Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is a federal fee area and entrance passes are required for all refuge users. Fees collected are used to directly assist with providing safe and meaningful experiences to refuge visitors, including improvement to the refuge's roads, parking lots, trails, publications, and other maintenance to visitor facilities.
**Refuge Pass Options**
*   $5.00 for a daily pass per vehicle. Valid for seven days only at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge.  
*   $15.00 for a vehicle annual pass. Valid only at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge.  
*   Commercial Vehicles: $5.00 for 9 or fewer passengers, $25.00 for 10-25 passengers, and $50.00 for 26 or more passengers.
**Where to Buy Your Pass**
A variety of passes can be purchased or obtained in-person onsite including refuge specific passes, Federal Duck Stamps, and America the Beautiful interagency passes (Annual, Senior, Access, Military, 4th Grade, or Volunteer). Learn more about America the Beautiful Passes.
*   Visit Recreation.gov to purchase a daily or annual Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge digital pass  
*   Okefenokee Adventures, Folkston, GA. Call ahead to confirm pass inventory: 912-496-7156  
*   Okefenokee State Park, Fargo, GA. Call ahead to confirm pass inventory: 912-637-5274

*   Entrance fees are included in the Camping Permit fee.  
*   All passes admit the passholder and up to 3 adults (age 16 or older) in a single, private, non-commercial vehicle.

# Okefenokee
## About
The Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1937 to conserve the unique features of the Okefenokee Swamp and protect migratory birds. Spanning approximately 407,000 acres, it is the largest National Wildlife Refuge east of the Mississippi River and is recognized as a Wetland of International Importance. The refuge is world-renowned for its pristine freshwater wetland ecosystem and provides critical habitat for threatened and endangered species like the red-cockaded woodpecker and indigo snake.

# Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge
## Outstanding Universal Value
The ONWR was established in 1937 by Executive Order, and 87% of it was classified as a National Wilderness Area in 1974 under the Wilderness Act by Congress and designated as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, thus providing for strict protection. The ONWR is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), in partnership with private enterprises that provide visitor services. Management is guided by a 15-year Comprehensive Conservation Plan (CCP) to maintain its ecological integrity and manage visitation, with an update expected at the time of inscription. The property is effectively protected through robust federal legislation at the time of nomination, including the National Environmental Policy Act (1970), Endangered Species Act (1973), Fish and Wildlife Act (1959), Clean Water Act (1977), Archaeological Resources Protection Act (1979), and Executive Order 13007 Indian Sacred Sites (1996), among others. Any reforms to the applicable legislation and the CCP need to ensure adequate protection for the attributes sustaining the Outstanding Universal Value of the property.
With the ONWR being of great historical, cultural, and spiritual significance for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, among other Indigenous Peoples, collaboration has grown between the ONWR management authorities and the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the years leading up to the nomination. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation has identified 74 ancestral burial mounds within the ONWR and aim to have the area declared Traditional Cultural Property under the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation considers it indispensable that cultural heritage values of the ONWR be recognized and appropriately protected alongside its natural values. It is thus important to reflect these values in the management framework of the property. The collection, storage, and disclosure of specific information and locations of sacred sites within the ONWR should be treated with sensitivity and led by the Indigenous Peoples concerned.

Title: Flashback Florida: Before the World Noticed Okefenokee Swamp

## **Why is the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge important?**
The Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is one of the world’s largest intact subtropical freshwater peatland ecosystems and now holds one of conservation’s highest honors: UNESCO World Heritage Site status. While many people think of the Okefenokee as a Georgia landmark, nearly 20 percent of the refuge’s 371,445 acres lie within Florida, making it Florida’s second UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The UNESCO designation recognizes the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge for its extraordinary ecological value. The refuge supports hundreds of species of fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals while protecting the headwaters of both the Suwannee River and the St. Marys River. Its wetlands filter water, store carbon, reduce flooding, and provide critical habitat that benefits wildlife across both Florida and Georgia.
But this international recognition didn’t happen overnight.
Long before UNESCO recognized the Okefenokee’s global importance, Americans were already working to protect it. In 1937, President Franklin D. Roosevelt established the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge to conserve the swamp’s wildlife and unique habitats after decades of logging and drainage proposals threatened the landscape. Nearly nine decades later, that decision stands as one of the Southeast’s most significant conservation successes.
> “This designation shows the deep roots of Florida’s conservation commitment,” Daphne Wood, Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida Board Member.
Today, the refuge remains a sanctuary for countless species, including American alligators, black bears, red-cockaded woodpeckers, sandhill cranes, river otters, and hundreds of other native animals. Its blackwater wetlands, cypress forests, wet prairies, and floating peat beds continue to function much as they have for thousands of years, sustaining biodiversity while protecting one of the Southeast’s most important freshwater ecosystems.

## **Why should Floridians care about the Okefenokee?**
For Floridians, the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is much more than a neighboring refuge. Approximately one-fifth of the swamp lies within Florida, where it contributes to the headwaters of the Suwannee River, one of the state’s most iconic waterways. Protecting the Okefenokee helps safeguard Florida’s water resources, wildlife habitat, outdoor recreation, and natural heritage.
For many Floridians, the Okefenokee has also inspired a lifelong appreciation for wildlife. Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida Executive Director Nick Wiley is one of them.
> “I grew up in south Georgia with this now World Heritage Site almost in my backyard,” Wiley said. “Visiting Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge when I was a kid made me want to be a wildlife biologist.”
His story reflects the lasting impact protected places can have. Generations of visitors have paddled the Okefenokee’s blackwater trails, listened to the calls of sandhill cranes at sunrise, and watched alligators glide through cypress-lined channels. Experiences like these don’t just create memories. They inspire future conservationists, scientists, land managers, and advocates who carry that stewardship forward.
Today, the UNESCO World Heritage Site designation places the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge alongside some of the world’s most celebrated natural landscapes. It is also the first National Wildlife Refuge in the United States to receive UNESCO World Heritage status, bringing international recognition to a place that Floridians and Georgians have treasured and protected for generations.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Is part of the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge in Florida?**
Yes. Nearly **20 percent of the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge lies within Florida**, making it Florida’s second UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Florida portion contributes to the headwaters of the Suwannee River and provides important habitat for native wildlife.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Why was the Okefenokee designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site?**
UNESCO recognized the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge because it is one of the world’s largest intact subtropical freshwater peatland ecosystems. Its exceptional biodiversity, ecological processes, and globally significant wetlands make it worthy of international recognition.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Why is the Okefenokee important to Florida?**
The Okefenokee helps protect the headwaters of the Suwannee River, supports hundreds of native wildlife species, improves water quality, stores carbon, and preserves outdoor recreation opportunities that benefit Floridians and future generations.

# Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge
## Outstanding Universal Value
The ONWR was established in 1937 by Executive Order, and 87% of it was classified as a National Wilderness Area in 1974 under the Wilderness Act by Congress and designated as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, thus providing for strict protection. The ONWR is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), in partnership with private enterprises that provide visitor services. Management is guided by a 15-year Comprehensive Conservation Plan (CCP) to maintain its ecological integrity and manage visitation, with an update expected at the time of inscription. The property is effectively protected through robust federal legislation at the time of nomination, including the National Environmental Policy Act (1970), Endangered Species Act (1973), Fish and Wildlife Act (1959), Clean Water Act (1977), Archaeological Resources Protection Act (1979), and Executive Order 13007 Indian Sacred Sites (1996), among others. Any reforms to the applicable legislation and the CCP need to ensure adequate protection for the attributes sustaining the Outstanding Universal Value of the property.
With the ONWR being of great historical, cultural, and spiritual significance for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, among other Indigenous Peoples, collaboration has grown between the ONWR management authorities and the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the years leading up to the nomination. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation has identified 74 ancestral burial mounds within the ONWR and aim to have the area declared Traditional Cultural Property under the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation considers it indispensable that cultural heritage values of the ONWR be recognized and appropriately protected alongside its natural values. It is thus important to reflect these values in the management framework of the property. The collection, storage, and disclosure of specific information and locations of sacred sites within the ONWR should be treated with sensitivity and led by the Indigenous Peoples concerned.

# Okefenokee
## Plan Your Visit
*   March to October: Open daily 30 minutes before sunrise to 7:30 p.m.  
*   November to February: Open daily 30 minutes before sunrise to 5:30 p.m.
**Suwannee River Sill, The Pocket, and Kingfisher Landing**
Open daily from sunrise to sunset.
**All boats must be off the water no later than**:
*   March to October: 6:00 pm  
*   November to February: 4:00 pm
Visit Okefenokee State Park for state park specific hours.
Pass Details
Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is a federal fee area and entrance passes are required for all refuge users. Fees collected are used to directly assist with providing safe and meaningful experiences to refuge visitors, including improvement to the refuge's roads, parking lots, trails, publications, and other maintenance to visitor facilities.
**Refuge Pass Options**
*   $5.00 for a daily pass per vehicle. Valid for seven days only at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge.  
*   $15.00 for a vehicle annual pass. Valid only at Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge.  
*   Commercial Vehicles: $5.00 for 9 or fewer passengers, $25.00 for 10-25 passengers, and $50.00 for 26 or more passengers.
**Where to Buy Your Pass**
A variety of passes can be purchased or obtained in-person onsite including refuge specific passes, Federal Duck Stamps, and America the Beautiful interagency passes (Annual, Senior, Access, Military, 4th Grade, or Volunteer). Learn more about America the Beautiful Passes.
*   Visit Recreation.gov to purchase a daily or annual Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge digital pass  
*   Okefenokee Adventures, Folkston, GA. Call ahead to confirm pass inventory: 912-496-7156  
*   Okefenokee State Park, Fargo, GA. Call ahead to confirm pass inventory: 912-637-5274  
*   Fee Machine (located on Suwannee Canal Road before entering Suwannee Canal Recreation Area)
**Additional Details**

## Plan Your Visit
*   Entrance fees are waived for visitors during Fee Free Days (see below) or if the visitor is in possession of a current and signed Federal Duck Stamp or America the Beautiful Interagency Pass.  
*   Entrance fees are included in the Suwannee Canal Recreation Area Hunt Permit fee.  
*   Entrance fees are included in the Camping Permit fee.  
*   All passes admit the passholder and up to 3 adults (age 16 or older) in a single, private, non-commercial vehicle.  
*   Please be prepared to show your hard copy pass or digital pass on your mobile device. We recommend that you print out or download your Recreation.gov pass on your mobile device in advance of your visit as cellular service may be limited.

# Okefenokee
## About
The Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge was established in 1937 to conserve the unique features of the Okefenokee Swamp and protect migratory birds. Spanning approximately 407,000 acres, it is the largest National Wildlife Refuge east of the Mississippi River and is recognized as a Wetland of International Importance. The refuge is world-renowned for its pristine freshwater wetland ecosystem and provides critical habitat for threatened and endangered species like the red-cockaded woodpecker and indigo snake.

# Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge
## Outstanding Universal Value
The ONWR was established in 1937 by Executive Order, and 87% of it was classified as a National Wilderness Area in 1974 under the Wilderness Act by Congress and designated as part of the National Wilderness Preservation System, thus providing for strict protection. The ONWR is managed by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS), in partnership with private enterprises that provide visitor services. Management is guided by a 15-year Comprehensive Conservation Plan (CCP) to maintain its ecological integrity and manage visitation, with an update expected at the time of inscription. The property is effectively protected through robust federal legislation at the time of nomination, including the National Environmental Policy Act (1970), Endangered Species Act (1973), Fish and Wildlife Act (1959), Clean Water Act (1977), Archaeological Resources Protection Act (1979), and Executive Order 13007 Indian Sacred Sites (1996), among others. Any reforms to the applicable legislation and the CCP need to ensure adequate protection for the attributes sustaining the Outstanding Universal Value of the property.
With the ONWR being of great historical, cultural, and spiritual significance for the Muscogee (Creek) Nation, among other Indigenous Peoples, collaboration has grown between the ONWR management authorities and the Muscogee (Creek) Nation in the years leading up to the nomination. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation has identified 74 ancestral burial mounds within the ONWR and aim to have the area declared Traditional Cultural Property under the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. The Muscogee (Creek) Nation considers it indispensable that cultural heritage values of the ONWR be recognized and appropriately protected alongside its natural values. It is thus important to reflect these values in the management framework of the property. The collection, storage, and disclosure of specific information and locations of sacred sites within the ONWR should be treated with sensitivity and led by the Indigenous Peoples concerned.

## **Why is the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge important?**
The Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is one of the world’s largest intact subtropical freshwater peatland ecosystems and now holds one of conservation’s highest honors: UNESCO World Heritage Site status. While many people think of the Okefenokee as a Georgia landmark, nearly 20 percent of the refuge’s 371,445 acres lie within Florida, making it Florida’s second UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The UNESCO designation recognizes the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge for its extraordinary ecological value. The refuge supports hundreds of species of fish, birds, reptiles, amphibians, and mammals while protecting the headwaters of both the Suwannee River and the St. Marys River. Its wetlands filter water, store carbon, reduce flooding, and provide critical habitat that benefits wildlife across both Florida and Georgia.
But this international recognition didn’t happen overnight.
Long before UNESCO recognized the Okefenokee’s global importance, Americans were already working to protect it. In 1937, President Franklin D. Roosevelt established the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge to conserve the swamp’s wildlife and unique habitats after decades of logging and drainage proposals threatened the landscape. Nearly nine decades later, that decision stands as one of the Southeast’s most significant conservation successes.
> “This designation shows the deep roots of Florida’s conservation commitment,” Daphne Wood, Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida Board Member.
Today, the refuge remains a sanctuary for countless species, including American alligators, black bears, red-cockaded woodpeckers, sandhill cranes, river otters, and hundreds of other native animals. Its blackwater wetlands, cypress forests, wet prairies, and floating peat beds continue to function much as they have for thousands of years, sustaining biodiversity while protecting one of the Southeast’s most important freshwater ecosystems.

## **Why should Floridians care about the Okefenokee?**
For Floridians, the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge is much more than a neighboring refuge. Approximately one-fifth of the swamp lies within Florida, where it contributes to the headwaters of the Suwannee River, one of the state’s most iconic waterways. Protecting the Okefenokee helps safeguard Florida’s water resources, wildlife habitat, outdoor recreation, and natural heritage.
For many Floridians, the Okefenokee has also inspired a lifelong appreciation for wildlife. Fish & Wildlife Foundation of Florida Executive Director Nick Wiley is one of them.
> “I grew up in south Georgia with this now World Heritage Site almost in my backyard,” Wiley said. “Visiting Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge when I was a kid made me want to be a wildlife biologist.”
His story reflects the lasting impact protected places can have. Generations of visitors have paddled the Okefenokee’s blackwater trails, listened to the calls of sandhill cranes at sunrise, and watched alligators glide through cypress-lined channels. Experiences like these don’t just create memories. They inspire future conservationists, scientists, land managers, and advocates who carry that stewardship forward.
Today, the UNESCO World Heritage Site designation places the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge alongside some of the world’s most celebrated natural landscapes. It is also the first National Wildlife Refuge in the United States to receive UNESCO World Heritage status, bringing international recognition to a place that Floridians and Georgians have treasured and protected for generations.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Is part of the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge in Florida?**
Yes. Nearly **20 percent of the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge lies within Florida**, making it Florida’s second UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Florida portion contributes to the headwaters of the Suwannee River and provides important habitat for native wildlife.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Why was the Okefenokee designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site?**
UNESCO recognized the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge because it is one of the world’s largest intact subtropical freshwater peatland ecosystems. Its exceptional biodiversity, ecological processes, and globally significant wetlands make it worthy of international recognition.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**
### **Why is the Okefenokee important to Florida?**
The Okefenokee helps protect the headwaters of the Suwannee River, supports hundreds of native wildlife species, improves water quality, stores carbon, and preserves outdoor recreation opportunities that benefit Floridians and future generations.

Source: https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/196/
Title: Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4
**Brief****Synthesis**
Located in the Mosquitia region of Northeastern Honduras, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is the largest protected area in the country with 350,000 hectares. The property protects the entire watershed of the Río Plátano all the way from the headwaters in the mountains to the river mouth on the Caribbean Coast. Adding to its importance, the property is an integral part of a significantly larger conservation complex encompassing Tawahka Asangni Biosphere Reserve and Patuca National Park, among other protected areas. Taken as a whole, the conservation complex in Northeastern Honduras is contiguous with Bosawas Biosphere Reserve in neighbouring Nicaragua, jointly constituting the largest contiguous forest area in Latin America north of the Amazon. Besides the remarkable dense rainforests in the mountains, there is a highly diverse array of distinct ecosystems in the coastal lowlands, including wetlands, savannah and coastal lagoons. Recognised as a nature conservation gem, the property also harbours notable archaeological and cultural values, with numerous Pre-Columbian sites and petroglyphs, as well as the living cultures of the various local and indigenous communities. Indigenous peoples and peoples of African descent in and around Río Plátano include the Pech, Tawahka, Miskito and Garífuna, living alongside the Mestizo (Ladino) population.

The property boasts an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems and species. For example, 586 species of vascular plants have been reported in the low lands of the reserve. The over 721 species of vertebrates comprise more than half of all mammals known to occur in Honduras and include the critically endangered Mexican Spider Monkey, the endangered Central American Tapir, the vulnerable Giant Anteater and West Indian Manatee, as well as the near-threatened Jaguar and White-lipped Peccary. The endangered Great Green Macaw, the vulnerable Great Curassow and the near-threatened Guiana Crested Eagle and harpy eagle stand out among the impressive 411 documented species of birds. Taken together, reptiles and amphibians total about 108 species, with several species of poisonous snakes and 4 species marine turtles (Loggerhead, Leatherback, green turtle and hawksbill turtle) . Freshwater fish include the economically important migratory Bobo Mullet or Cuyamel.**_Criterion (vii):_**The natural beauty of Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is a function of the variety of the terrain and landscape types and features. Within its boundaries, the property harbours densely forested mountains reaching 1,418 m.a.s.l. at Punta Piedra, transitioning into savannahs, patches of pine forest and vast wetlands towards the coastal plains of the Caribbean Sea. Along the coast, there are spectacular lagoons, namely Laguna Brus and Laguna Ibans, both full of wildlife, boasting major bird colonies and serving as nurseries for fish and many other forms of aquatic life. Another characteristic element of the landscape are the many rivers and creeks, namely the eponymous Río Plátano and the Sico, Sikre Kipahni, Uhra and Tilasunta Rivers.

**_Criterion (viii):_**The property comprises two main geomorphological areas. These are the steep mountain range harbouring the headwaters of Río Plátano and the flat to undulating coastal plains. The latter is composed of terraces of recent marine sediments and partly underlain by a belt of infertile deeply weathered Pleistocene quartz sandy gravels. The Río Plátano meanders for some 45 kilometres through the lowlands forming ox-bow lakes, backwater swamps and natural levees. At about 100 m.a.s.l inland the foothills begin abruptly. The rugged granite mountains, which rise to Punta Piedra at 1,418 m.a.s.l. have many steep ridges, remarkable rock formations such as Pico Dama, a 150 metre pinnacle, and many waterfalls, one reaching 150 metres in height. Two thirds of the Plátano River run through a rugged part of the mountains with long stretches of white water. In one cataract in a deep forested gorge the river disappears under massive boulders. The mountains are part of the Cordillera Central, which corresponds to what was the Honduras Intercontinental Depression, during the Cretaceous period.
**_Criterion (ix):_** As one of a quickly decreasing number of major river basins the Plátano River, the heart of the property, continues to flow freely from its mountainous headwaters to the Sea. Along the altitudinal range the property connects a huge variety of very different ecosystems and habitats. The ecological linkages between these ecosystems and corresponding processes continue to be largely intact at the landscape level. Starting from the Caribbean Sea, there are estuarine and marine systems, sandy beaches, coastal lagoons of varying salinity, mangrove swamps, and pine savannah. Along the many rivers and creeks, there are broadleaf gallery forest traversing the savannahs and serving as natural corridors. The bulk of the property, however, are dense tropical rainforests covering the mountain ranges inland with smaller areas of rare elfin forest on the highest ridges.

**_Criterion (x):_**As a globally important stronghold of biodiversity Río Plátano harbours at least 586 species of vascular plants in its diverse habitats and there may still be species new to science in remote parts of the property. Across virtually all taxonomic groups, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is home to impressive proportions of the fauna of the entire country, in many cases well over half of the number of species occurring. The over 721 species of vertebrates include more than half of all mammals known in Honduras, such as the critically endangered Mexican Spider Monkey, the endangered Central American Tapir, the vulnerable Giant Anteater and the West Indian Manatee, as well as the near-threatened Jaguar and White-lipped Peccary. Other charismatic species are Puma, Ocelot, Jaguarundi and Margay, Neotropical Otter, White-throated Capuchin Monkey and Mantled Howler Monkey. The endangered Great Green Macaw, the vulnerable Great Curassow and Scarlet Macaw and the near-threatened Guiana Crested Eagle and harpy eagle stand out among the impressive 411 documented species of birds, along with Jabiru, King Vulture and the majestic Harpy Eagle. The 108 species of reptiles and amphibians comprise several rare poisonous snakes and 4 species marine turtles (Loggerhead, Leatherback, green turtle and hawksbill turtle)
**Integrity**
The Reserve contains a rich variety of ecosystems (28 terrestrial ecosystems and 5 coastal marine), habitats and species of global conservation importance. The Plátano River is a major landscape feature and corridor connecting all the landscape elements from the rugged mountains to the coastal plains. Granting a conservation status to the entire watershed from the headwaters to the river mouth is an ideal set-up from a conservation perspective.
**Protection and Management requirements**

Due to its archaeological importance parts of the Río Plátano basin became subject to protection efforts long before the nature conservation values were formally recognised. In 1960, Ciudad Blanca Archaeological Reserve was created, later re-classified as an Archaeological National Park in 1969, which Río Plátano formally remains to this day. In terms of nature conservation, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve was originally designated in 1980 by Decree and substantially extended in 1997 by a further Decree. Likewise in 1980, the area was internationally recognized as a biosphere reserve, prior to the inscription on the World Heritage List in 1982. The legal umbrella for all formally protected areas in Honduras is the national General Environmental Law, which establishes the national protected areas system. Further regulations are specified in a corresponding by-law. More recently, the Forest, Protected Areas and Wildlife Law came into force, jointly with the establishment of a new governmental authority for the management and conservation of forests, nature and wildlife. The legal framework supports co-management agreements and involvement of civil society at all levels.
A major management instrument is zonation to distinguish areas requiring strict protection and areas of controlled use of natural resources.
Despite the strong legal protection, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve has long been suffering from human pressure threatening its integrity. Forests continue to be logged and converted to pasture, agricultural encroachment and illegal resource extraction are widespread. While systematic law enforcement is needed, there is a consensus that addressing the complex environmental challenges requires integrated development strategies, policies and measures for the entire region across sectors and disciplines and involving local communities. The property is located in a remote region of rural poverty, where a balance between conservation and development is needed. Regulation of land tenure and access to resources and effective co-management and sharing of power in decision-making are seen as promising instruments to this effect.
Indigenous peoples in the Mosquitia continue to have a close relationship with their natural environment, as expressed in myths and beliefs but also knowledge and practices. While not a guarantee for sustainable resource use, this can make a valuable contribution to conservation. Ambitious plans for hydroelectric development on nearby rivers may also entail risks for the conservation values and local livelihoods, therefore requiring careful analysis. Future management of Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve should also promote an enhanced understanding and protection of the many archaeological sites hidden in the dense forests.

opened.information:
Source: https://news.mongabay.com/2021/05/in-the-honduran-rio-platano-biosphere-reserve-an-illegal-road-for-cattle-and-drugs/
Title: In the Honduran Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve, an illegal road for cattle and drugs
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
*   _Multiple sources, backed by satellite data, say an illegal road is being cut through the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve in Honduras, a UNESCO World Heritage Site._  
*   _Sources say the road will facilitate land invasions into the biosphere and is likely to be used as a drug-trafficking route._  
*   _The road has created divisions between Indigenous groups, with the Bakinasta Miskito denouncing its presence and demanding the government step in to halt it._  
*   _Despite knowing about the road for more than a year, the Honduran government has not taken definitive action to enforce the law._
Beginning along Honduras’s northeastern coastline and stretching south into its dense interior rainforests lies the Río Plátano Biosphere. Named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982, the Río Plátano is one of the most impressive ecosystems on the planet. Rivers swoop in wide arches through the forest, which is home to more than 721 known species of vertebrates, including jaguars, giant anteaters, and great green macaws. To its far south, the Río Plátano overlaps with Indigenous land reserves that spill across the border into neighboring Nicaragua’s Bosawas Biosphere Reserve.
In all, the 630,000-hectare (1.56-million-acre) protected reserve, along with its 200,000-hectare (494,000-acre) buffer zone and adjoining Indigenous territories, comprises some of the last intact remnants of the Mesoamerican rainforest, which once encompassed wide swaths of Central America. In recent years, the Río Plátano has also suffered from skyrocketing rates of deforestation, as illegal invasions by cattle ranchers, loggers, and drug traffickers have threatened the integrity of the biosphere.
Now, Mongabay has obtained evidence of an illegal road being cut directly through the Río Plátano’s buffer zone and into the heart of the Indigenous territories. Indigenous leaders in the area say the road is the “greatest threat in the Río Plátano” and accuse the Honduran government of turning a blind eye to their legal obligations to halt it.
“The road has been built as a tool for illicit actors, and will be used to traffic drugs, wood, and other products,” one leader told Mongabay.
Aerial view of Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve in Honduras. Image by Panthera.

Mongabay verified the existence of the road through multiple sources in the region, including officials who work for agencies with supervisory authority over the biosphere. According to those sources, the financiers of the road are powerful local businessmen and politicians with purported ties to drug traffickers. Due to the risks associated with speaking publicly about the road, Mongabay agreed to protect their identities.
“We know that very powerful people are among those building the highway, including drug traffickers and large cattle ranchers,” said one Honduran government official with direct knowledge of issues related to the Río Plátano.
According to Mongabay’s sources, the construction of the road picked up steam beginning early last year and accelerated during the COVID-19 pandemic. Satellite data show that the road begins in Honduras’s central department of Olancho, and has now crossed Indigenous Tawahka territory, extending east through the Río Plátano’s buffer zone and into Bakinasta lands owned by the Miskito Indigenous group in the department of Gracias a Dios. Conservationists who work in the region say that its presence is an immediate threat to the Río Plátano biosphere and will provide easy access to land speculators seeking to establish cattle ranches and agricultural operations.
“This road will inevitably both create a deforestation corridor across the entire Miskito forest, be used as a conduit for drugs and other illicit goods, and put at risk Indigenous territories all the way from east to west,” said an advocate with experience working in the region.
The initial portion of the road was built in 2008, but sources told Mongabay that it was rapidly extended through the Río Plátano during the pandemic, as Indigenous leaders have been pressured to sign illegal agreements permitting its construction. While some elements of the Tawahka group are said to be supportive of the road due to the access it opens up to health facilities and economic opportunities in nearby cities, documents reviewed by Mongabay show that the neighboring Miskito are staunchly opposed to its presence, fearing that it will lead to a flood of land grabs and violent incursions onto their land.
“This assembly declares the interdepartmental highway project unwelcome and considers it a direct threat to our territory and natural resources,” wrote the Miskito Bakinasta’s territorial council in a declaration sent to the Honduran prosecutor responsible for Indigenous affairs last year.
A satellite image of the southern buffer zone in the Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve from January 4, 2020.

A subsequent image of the same area taken on April 23, 2020. The newly constructed road is visible as a thin blue line below the river.
Despite the clear illegality of the road and the threat it poses to the integrity of the Río Plátano, so far the Honduran government has failed to halt its construction despite having incontrovertible knowledge of its presence, Mongabay’s sources said.
“The government’s authorities have moved very passively,” said the Indigenous leader. “They haven’t acted although there is a legal framework that empowers the armed forces to institute forest conservation and protect life in the Río Plátano because it is a world heritage site.”
Lands owned by the Miskito group have come under threat from speculators and _colonos,_ or “settlers,” in Honduras as well as neighboring Nicaragua. Last year, the Oakland Institute published a report indicating that at least 40 Indigenous people have been killed in land disputes in Nicaragua since 2015. Advocates say they fear the road will accelerate the presence of similar threats in Honduran Miskito territories. At least four killings have already taken place in communities along its path since last year, with the assailants arriving on motorized ATVs and leaving via the newly constructed portion of the road.
“The danger is very, very clear here,” said the advocate. “These are not people to be messed with.”
The presence of the road and the Honduran government’s refusal to shut it down is a window into the country’s struggles with corruption and impunity. In 2019, President Juan Orlando Hernández’s brother was convicted of drug trafficking in New York, and evidence presented by prosecutors in a separate trial implicated Hernández himself in the illicit trade.
“It’s very clear that political elites who can also be connected to the illicit trades exert a lot of influence on the attorney general’s office,” said Stephen Dudley, co-director of Insight Crime. “We did a story that was chronicling all the different ways in which members of the national party were connected to illicit activities, everything from embezzling funds for their own campaigns to drug trafficking and illegal timber trafficking. And all of these interests are being serviced by a weak and corrupted state.”
The Rio Platano Biosphere Reserve is home to wildlife like jaguar. Photo credit: Rhett A. Butler.

According to Insight Crime’s research, drug trafficking through Honduras and the Río Plátano has spiked in recent years, as smugglers lean more heavily on routes that head inland from the coastline through the rainforest and northward into Guatemala and Mexico. A road traversing the Río Plátano would be a boon to traffickers, allowing them to more easily transport shipments through the remote region away from prying eyes and interdiction efforts.
“This is a dangerous subject,” said Mongabay’s source in the Honduran government. “There have been big drug traffickers in the northern part of the Río Plátano, including the Amador, who we believe are behind the road because the access route is faster.”
The ICF and representatives of Honduras’s environmental prosecutor’s office are said to have made repeated visits to the road, but so far the political willpower to execute arrests or take strong action has not been present. Neither the ICF nor the public prosecutor’s office responded to Mongabay’s requests for comment.
“We know that some deputies or politicians of the current government have properties in Río Plátano or the Tawahka biosphere, so the road is obviously convenient for them,” said the official. “We believe that there are strong political links between the opening of the road and cattle ranchers, because many politicians in Olancho are themselves cattle ranchers.”
Location of the road. Satellite image credit: Planet.
As the Bakinasta Miskito continue to lodge protests without follow-up action by the authorities, fears are growing that elements within the Honduran government have decided to allow the road to remain despite the threat it poses to the Río Plátano.
“It seems like they are expecting or waiting for some political decision,” said a Tegucigalpa-based conservation advocate. “They may leave the case there forever without doing something. That would be the worst-case scenario.”
For forests and wildlife inside the Río Plátano, along with the Indigenous communities living on its edges, that could spell disaster.
“This is happening because of institutional abandonment,” said the official. “Now these cattle ranchers, drug traffickers, and politicians have done what they want in the Moskitia area and as a result of that we have this road.”
_Banner image: Stills taken from a video of the road’s construction in Tawahka territory last summer._

**Brief****Synthesis**
Located in the Mosquitia region of Northeastern Honduras, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is the largest protected area in the country with 350,000 hectares. The property protects the entire watershed of the Río Plátano all the way from the headwaters in the mountains to the river mouth on the Caribbean Coast. Adding to its importance, the property is an integral part of a significantly larger conservation complex encompassing Tawahka Asangni Biosphere Reserve and Patuca National Park, among other protected areas. Taken as a whole, the conservation complex in Northeastern Honduras is contiguous with Bosawas Biosphere Reserve in neighbouring Nicaragua, jointly constituting the largest contiguous forest area in Latin America north of the Amazon. Besides the remarkable dense rainforests in the mountains, there is a highly diverse array of distinct ecosystems in the coastal lowlands, including wetlands, savannah and coastal lagoons. Recognised as a nature conservation gem, the property also harbours notable archaeological and cultural values, with numerous Pre-Columbian sites and petroglyphs, as well as the living cultures of the various local and indigenous communities. Indigenous peoples and peoples of African descent in and around Río Plátano include the Pech, Tawahka, Miskito and Garífuna, living alongside the Mestizo (Ladino) population.
texts.1: The property boasts an extraordinary diversity of ecosystems and species. For example, 586 species of vascular plants have been reported in the low lands of the reserve. The over 721 species of vertebrates comprise more than half of all mammals known to occur in Honduras and include the critically endangered Mexican Spider Monkey, the endangered Central American Tapir, the vulnerable Giant Anteater and West Indian Manatee, as well as the near-threatened Jaguar and White-lipped Peccary. The endangered Great Green Macaw, the vulnerable Great Curassow and the near-threatened Guiana Crested Eagle and harpy eagle stand out among the impressive 411 documented species of birds. Taken together, reptiles and amphibians total about 108 species, with several species of poisonous snakes and 4 species marine turtles (Loggerhead, Leatherback, green turtle and hawksbill turtle) . Freshwater fish include the economically important migratory Bobo Mullet or Cuyamel.**_Criterion (vii):_**The natural beauty of Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is a function of the variety of the terrain and landscape types and features. Within its boundaries, the property harbours densely forested mountains reaching 1,418 m.a.s.l. at Punta Piedra, transitioning into savannahs, patches of pine forest and vast wetlands towards the coastal plains of the Caribbean Sea. Along the coast, there are spectacular lagoons, namely Laguna Brus and Laguna Ibans, both full of wildlife, boasting major bird colonies and serving as nurseries for fish and many other forms of aquatic life. Another characteristic element of the landscape are the many rivers and creeks, namely the eponymous Río Plátano and the Sico, Sikre Kipahni, Uhra and Tilasunta Rivers.
texts.2:
**_Criterion (viii):_**The property comprises two main geomorphological areas. These are the steep mountain range harbouring the headwaters of Río Plátano and the flat to undulating coastal plains. The latter is composed of terraces of recent marine sediments and partly underlain by a belt of infertile deeply weathered Pleistocene quartz sandy gravels. The Río Plátano meanders for some 45 kilometres through the lowlands forming ox-bow lakes, backwater swamps and natural levees. At about 100 m.a.s.l inland the foothills begin abruptly. The rugged granite mountains, which rise to Punta Piedra at 1,418 m.a.s.l. have many steep ridges, remarkable rock formations such as Pico Dama, a 150 metre pinnacle, and many waterfalls, one reaching 150 metres in height. Two thirds of the Plátano River run through a rugged part of the mountains with long stretches of white water. In one cataract in a deep forested gorge the river disappears under massive boulders. The mountains are part of the Cordillera Central, which corresponds to what was the Honduras Intercontinental Depression, during the Cretaceous period.
**_Criterion (ix):_** As one of a quickly decreasing number of major river basins the Plátano River, the heart of the property, continues to flow freely from its mountainous headwaters to the Sea. Along the altitudinal range the property connects a huge variety of very different ecosystems and habitats. The ecological linkages between these ecosystems and corresponding processes continue to be largely intact at the landscape level. Starting from the Caribbean Sea, there are estuarine and marine systems, sandy beaches, coastal lagoons of varying salinity, mangrove swamps, and pine savannah. Along the many rivers and creeks, there are broadleaf gallery forest traversing the savannahs and serving as natural corridors. The bulk of the property, however, are dense tropical rainforests covering the mountain ranges inland with smaller areas of rare elfin forest on the highest ridges.
texts.3:
**_Criterion (x):_**As a globally important stronghold of biodiversity Río Plátano harbours at least 586 species of vascular plants in its diverse habitats and there may still be species new to science in remote parts of the property. Across virtually all taxonomic groups, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve is home to impressive proportions of the fauna of the entire country, in many cases well over half of the number of species occurring. The over 721 species of vertebrates include more than half of all mammals known in Honduras, such as the critically endangered Mexican Spider Monkey, the endangered Central American Tapir, the vulnerable Giant Anteater and the West Indian Manatee, as well as the near-threatened Jaguar and White-lipped Peccary. Other charismatic species are Puma, Ocelot, Jaguarundi and Margay, Neotropical Otter, White-throated Capuchin Monkey and Mantled Howler Monkey. The endangered Great Green Macaw, the vulnerable Great Curassow and Scarlet Macaw and the near-threatened Guiana Crested Eagle and harpy eagle stand out among the impressive 411 documented species of birds, along with Jabiru, King Vulture and the majestic Harpy Eagle. The 108 species of reptiles and amphibians comprise several rare poisonous snakes and 4 species marine turtles (Loggerhead, Leatherback, green turtle and hawksbill turtle)
**Integrity**
The Reserve contains a rich variety of ecosystems (28 terrestrial ecosystems and 5 coastal marine), habitats and species of global conservation importance. The Plátano River is a major landscape feature and corridor connecting all the landscape elements from the rugged mountains to the coastal plains. Granting a conservation status to the entire watershed from the headwaters to the river mouth is an ideal set-up from a conservation perspective.
**Protection and Management requirements**
texts.4:
Due to its archaeological importance parts of the Río Plátano basin became subject to protection efforts long before the nature conservation values were formally recognised. In 1960, Ciudad Blanca Archaeological Reserve was created, later re-classified as an Archaeological National Park in 1969, which Río Plátano formally remains to this day. In terms of nature conservation, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve was originally designated in 1980 by Decree and substantially extended in 1997 by a further Decree. Likewise in 1980, the area was internationally recognized as a biosphere reserve, prior to the inscription on the World Heritage List in 1982. The legal umbrella for all formally protected areas in Honduras is the national General Environmental Law, which establishes the national protected areas system. Further regulations are specified in a corresponding by-law. More recently, the Forest, Protected Areas and Wildlife Law came into force, jointly with the establishment of a new governmental authority for the management and conservation of forests, nature and wildlife. The legal framework supports co-management agreements and involvement of civil society at all levels.
A major management instrument is zonation to distinguish areas requiring strict protection and areas of controlled use of natural resources.
Despite the strong legal protection, Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve has long been suffering from human pressure threatening its integrity. Forests continue to be logged and converted to pasture, agricultural encroachment and illegal resource extraction are widespread. While systematic law enforcement is needed, there is a consensus that addressing the complex environmental challenges requires integrated development strategies, policies and measures for the entire region across sectors and disciplines and involving local communities. The property is located in a remote region of rural poverty, where a balance between conservation and development is needed. Regulation of land tenure and access to resources and effective co-management and sharing of power in decision-making are seen as promising instruments to this effect.
Indigenous peoples in the Mosquitia continue to have a close relationship with their natural environment, as expressed in myths and beliefs but also knowledge and practices. While not a guarantee for sustainable resource use, this can make a valuable contribution to conservation. Ambitious plans for hydroelectric development on nearby rivers may also entail risks for the conservation values and local livelihoods, therefore requiring careful analysis. Future management of Río Plátano Biosphere Reserve should also promote an enhanced understanding and protection of the many archaeological sites hidden in the dense forests.
